subject: mathematics
question_text: By using the matrix inversion method, solve x + y + z = 9, 2x + 5y + 7z = 52, 2x + y − z = 0.

mark_split.label: Write the system as AX = D and X = A⁻¹D
Find det A and check it is not zero
Transpose to Adj A and write A⁻¹
Multiply A⁻¹ by D and state the solution

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.51, chapter 5 MATRICES, Long Answer question 9(ii), matrix-inversion route. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+3+1+2 split gives three of the eight marks to the nine cofactors, because that is where most of the working and most of the errors are, and matches every other matrix-inversion answer in this unit. ONE CARD PER METHOD: the book asks this one system by matrix inversion, by Cramer's rule and by the Gauss-Jordan method, and this bank answers each method on its own card so that a student who opens one never has to read another. The siblings are ts_ipe_m1a_mat_cramer_x_y_z_9_2x5y7z52 and ts_ipe_m1a_mat_gauss_x_y_z_9_2x5y7z52, and all three land on the same solution x = 1, y = 3, z = 5. Working checked twice: det A was expanded along R₁ and again along C₁, both giving −4; A(Adj A) = (det A)I was checked on two entries before the inverse was used; and the solution was substituted back into all three original equations (9 = 9, 52 = 52, 0 = 0). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Matrices is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the matrix inversion method — say what you have to find first, how you build the inverse, what you multiply at the end, and how you check it.

steps.label: Write it as AX = D
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the plan as well as the matrices: the solution of AX = D is X = A⁻¹D, so everything after this line is about building A⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Write the PLAN as well as the matrices: X = A⁻¹D, so everything after is about building A⁻¹.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 52 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}

lines: The solution of AX = D is X = A⁻¹D.

recall.must_convey: That the system is written as AX = D and that its solution is X = A⁻¹D — so the inverse is what has to be found.
accept: write it as A X equals D so the solution is X equals A inverse D
put the system in matrix form and then X is A inverse times D
form A X and D and say the solution is A inverse into D
AX equals D form lo rasi, solution X equals A inverse D ani rasta
the coefficient matrix times the unknowns equals the constants so multiply by the inverse

steps.why: AX = D is solved by multiplying both sides on the LEFT by A⁻¹. Writing X = A⁻¹D at the start states the plan, and the plan is what the remaining marks pay for.
common_mistakes: Writing X = DA⁻¹; matrix multiplication does not commute, and that order does not even have matching sizes.
Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.
Missing a coefficient of 1 or −1 written with no number in front.

steps.label: Find det A
steps.margin_note: Second mark. det A is −4, non-zero, so A⁻¹ exists. Expand it a second time along a different row or column — a wrong determinant is divided into every entry of the inverse, so it spoils all three answers at once.
steps.memory_tip: det A = −4, non-zero, so A⁻¹ exists. Expand it twice, and write the non-zero check down.

recall.must_convey: That det A is computed, comes to −4, and that being non-zero is what guarantees A⁻¹ exists.
accept: find the determinant of A which is minus four and since it is not zero the inverse exists
compute det A and check it is non zero so A is non singular
expand the determinant of the coefficient matrix twice, it is not zero so the inverse exists
det A kanukoni, zero kaadu kabatti inverse untundi
the determinant must be non zero for A inverse to exist

steps.why: A⁻¹ is Adj A divided by det A. A zero determinant would mean dividing by zero — which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse and this method would stop here.
common_mistakes: Computing det A but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong: plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Confusing det A with the trace or with the sum of a row.

steps.label: Find the cofactor matrix
steps.margin_note: Three marks, and the longest part of the question — nine 2×2 determinants. Cross out the entry's own row and column, take the determinant of what is left, then apply the sign for that position.
steps.memory_tip: Nine 2×2 determinants, with the sign board + − + / − + − / + − +. Cross out the entry's own row and column.
lines: Delete each entry's row and column, take the
2×2 determinant, then apply the sign board

recall.must_convey: That each cofactor is the 2×2 determinant left after deleting that entry's row and column, with the alternating plus-minus sign applied.
accept: for each entry delete its row and column take the two by two determinant and put the plus minus sign
find the nine cofactors using the minors with the alternating sign pattern
cross out the row and column of each entry and take the determinant of what is left with the correct sign
prathi entry ki row column teesesi, two by two determinant teeskoni sign pettali
build the cofactor matrix from the nine minors with signs plus minus plus

steps.why: A minor is just the smaller determinant. A cofactor is that minor with a sign attached, and the sign depends only on the position — which is why the board is worth memorising once rather than deriving nine times.
common_mistakes: Writing the minors and forgetting the sign board entirely.
Applying the signs to the wrong positions; the corners are all plus.
Deleting the wrong row or column for the off-diagonal entries.

steps.label: Transpose to get Adj A
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark, and the step most often skipped. This cofactor matrix is NOT symmetric, so the transpose really changes it — rows become columns. Then A⁻¹ is Adj A divided by det A, and one row of A times the columns of Adj A checks it before it is used.
steps.memory_tip: Adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix — the step most often skipped. Then divide by det A and check A(Adj A) = (det A)I.
lines: Adj A is the transpose of the cofactors:
Check A(Adj A) = (det A)I on the top row:
So A·A⁻¹ = I and the inverse is correct.

recall.must_convey: That the adjoint is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix, that A⁻¹ is the adjoint divided by det A, and that A times A⁻¹ is checked to be I.
accept: take the transpose of the cofactor matrix to get adj A then divide by det A to get the inverse
adjoint is the transpose of the cofactors and A inverse is adj A over det A
transpose the cofactor matrix, divide by the determinant, and check A into A inverse is the identity
cofactor matrix transpose teeste adj A vasthundi, det A tho divide cheste inverse
A inverse equals one by det A times the adjoint

steps.why: Forgetting the transpose gives a matrix that looks right and is wrong, and nothing later in the question will reveal it. Multiplying one row of A into one column of Adj A costs three products and proves the inverse before it is used.
common_mistakes: Using the cofactor matrix directly as the adjoint without transposing.
Dividing only one row by det A instead of the whole matrix.
Multiplying by det A instead of dividing.

steps.label: Multiply A⁻¹ by D
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Every product comes out negative and det A is −4, so all three answers are positive. Write the divisions out, then put the values back into the three original equations.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply row by column, divide every entry by det A, then put the three values back into the three original equations.
lines: X = A⁻¹D. Multiplying row by column:

recall.must_convey: That A⁻¹ is multiplied by D row against column, and that dividing by det A gives x = 1, y = 3, z = 5, checked in the original equations.
accept: multiply A inverse by D row into column and divide by det A to get the three values
do the matrix multiplication and then divide each entry by the determinant
X equals A inverse D so multiply out and read off x equals one y equals three z equals five
A inverse ni D tho multiply chesi det A tho divide cheste x y z vasthai
row into column multiplication gives the column matrix and that is the solution

steps.why: X comes out as a single column matrix, and its three entries ARE x, y and z in that order. Substituting them back into the original equations is the only check that catches a slip inside the cofactors.
common_mistakes: Multiplying column by row instead of row by column.
Dividing by det A only once instead of on every entry.
Stopping without substituting the three values back into all three equations.
